title: Pace as a variance lever: real but modest
headline_insight: Across the NBA's observed pace range (about 92 to 104 possessions), an 80% favorite's upset probability rises only from 19.5% at the fastest pace to 20.9% at the slowest -- a 1.4-point swing.
what_it_means: Fewer possessions mean fewer chances for the better team to separate, so the underdog's chances grow as pace slows -- the sqrt(N) scaling of a possession-margin model. But because real NBA pace barely moves game to game, the mechanical effect on any single matchup is small: a couple of upset-probability points, not a coin flip. A slow, grind-it-out game genuinely helps the underdog, just not by much.
how_to_read: Each curve fixes a favorite's strength at reference pace, then reprices its upset probability at every pace on the grid; the slow-minus-fast swing is the whole span of that effect.
why_it_matters: It quantifies a piece of basketball folklore -- 'slow it down to beat a better team' -- and shows the honest size of the effect, which matters for how much a live model should move when tempo runs hot or cold.
caveat: COUNTERFACTUAL floor: per-possession scoring margin and variance are held pace-invariant, so this isolates the mechanical variance effect only, not behavioral changes (teams that push pace may also change shot quality). Margin is assumed Normal (CLT over ~100 possessions), weaker for short in-game windows.
